sentences.text: The first accused in C.C.No.694 of 2009 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-II, Hosdurg, has filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1) (a) (i) r/w Section 2 (ia) (m) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 5 of Appendix-B item A.28.04 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and section 16 (1) (a) (ii) r/w 7 (iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 50 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class-II, Hosdurg
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.
The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 16.5.2009 at 10.30 a.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 600 grams of broken cashew nuts from the first accused.
The second accused was the distributor.
After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent for analysis to the Public Analyst.

Ext.P12 report of the Public Analyst would show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for dry fruits and nuts under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and was therefore adulterated.
It was further found that the first accused had no licence to sell the food articles.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW5 were examined and Exts.P1 to P34 were marked for the prosecution.
No evidence was adduced on the side of the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P12 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

sentences.text:
In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P12 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained under Section 16 (1) (a) (i) r/w Section 2 (ia) (m) and Section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 5 Appendix-B item No.A.28.04 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
However, the evidence on record would clearly show that the revision petitioner sold the food article without having a valid licence under the Rules.

Therefore, the courts below concurrently found that the revision petitioner committed the offence under Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) r/w Section 7 (iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Rule 50 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.

Having gone through the relevant inputs, I find no reason to interfere with the conviction passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1) (a)
(ii) r/w Section 7 (iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Rule 50 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.
The sentence awarded by the courts below for the said offence also does not warrant any interference by this Court.

In the result, this revision petition stands allowed in part, setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1) (a) (i) r/w Section 2 (ia) (m) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act r/w Rule 5 Appendix-B Item No.A.28.04 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and confirming the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) r/w 7 (iii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act and Rule 50 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.
The revision petitioner shall surrender before the court below on 1.3.2016 to suffer the sentence.

Sd/-
B. SUDHEENDRA KUMAR JUDGE Scl/14.01.2016
